title: Just watched Monster (2023) directed by Hirokazu Kore-eda - Question about the Ending

commenti.body: I think they are dead in the end, which is honestly a disappointing and outdated ending to a movie that has an otherwise truly brilliant script. The message seems to be that queer youth have no safe space in the real world and that they have to die to become truly free, and I’m not sure that’s an accurate, useful or compelling message to be telling in 2023, even in Japan, where LGBT rights and acceptance are lagging behind the West.

Agreed with you :( Nevertheless, I really loved the unravelling of all stories across the three acts, and how things can get misunderstood / miscommunicated (to maintain a certain level of traditional expectations / conformity in Japan).

The key detail for me, which I hope I remember correctly, is the gate they walk through at the end over the railway bridge that was shown to be closed and impossible to access earlier. So it is like they are in a different realm or whatever.

I was a bit disappointed by that ending in that it seemed arbitrary. I think it would have been better if they survived. I can't think of a reason in the film that they have to be dead at the end to tie into its themes. But in my limited experience with Japanese cinema it does seem like they lean heavily into tragic or "bad" endings (Kore-eda's Shoplifters maybe) and so maybe there is a cultural tradition being followed that is more distasteful for Western viewers?

I wonder if that is a Western reading of the ending and if tragic endings in Japanese storytelling mean something different? I only say bc they seem to be very prevalent and so maybe they perceive "bad" endings differently.

The story appears to take much inspiration from the novel by Miyazawa Kenji "Night on the Galactic Railroad" which also has had numerous queer readings. The ending is thematically very reminiscent which may explain the somewhat ambiguous ending.

"The message seems to be that queer youth have no safe space in the real world and that they have to die to become truly free" - that wasn't really my takeaway from this movie. 

I don't think this movie was focused on LGBTQ rights specifically, and I would not judge it on that standard. It was more a movie about secrets, understandings and misunderstandings, and the monsters we make of each other.

But say we take a laser-focused lens on LGBTQ rights. The rights and safe spaces for LGBTQ people have always been the ones that we have had to fight for and create for ourselves. These safe spaces are always at risk of erosion and destruction should we become complacent. Perhaps then the message was more a warning against complacency.

But even assuming you're right that the movie was trying to illustrate the "hopelessness" of LGBTQ existence, I also would not dismiss it as inaccurate - it depends a lot on cultural context. If you're a white person growing up in an accepting environment, your experience will be very different from a brown kid growing up in an ultra-religious family. Etc. I have no way of knowing the situation in Japan, but Kore-Eda mentioned at the Q&A at TIFF that Japan was really behind the times.

I am not Japanese myself but I live in Japan and saw the film with my Japanese boyfriend, who shared my take on the ending. As I said in my original comment, even given Japan's current climate of LGBT acceptance, which has a long way to go, the ending of the film felt overly pessimistic and a little outdated.

Uhm...as a queer woman I actually love this ending. It's the kindest ending I've ever found in movies and books and it's certainly my favorite. I remember being quite fascinated by the whole idea of rebirth at one point in my childhood and even believed I could pass into a whole new world any day, so the film sort of speaks to my childhood experience and makes me feel seen and loved. I'm not so knowledgeable about Japanese cinema and culture, but I also get a sense that Japanese films, books, and music lean quite heavily into what other cultures may see as "tragic", and in their culture "tragic" endings aren't necessarily sad nor pessimistic. Check out the song Pink Spider by Hide & Spread Beaver and you'll get what I mean. Maybe I see things this way cause I've always felt super lonely and excluded from all the good things in life and suicidal, and strangely enough, sometimes happy endings alienate me even more. Maybe people don't always need to be told they can be happy. Maybe they don't always want to be happy, or even if they want to they just...can't? Maybe they just need someone to acknowledge all their pain and hopelessness? The same way Minato shares one of his sneakers with Yori (it's actually my favorite scene in the film, and the moment I saw it, I knew I've finally found my favorite movie). It doesn't solve any problems, but what if Yori doesn't need a solution, a way out, just a companion? I don't always like tragic endings of course, but the ending of Monster is one that makes me feel hopeful, because the adults are always one step behind, and the children, despite being young and scared and unsure about so many things, keep choosing happiness and each other (remember the scene Yori risks more beatings by his abusive father just to tell Minato he lied about having a female crush? I feel like only children are capable of making such choices). The ending of Monster holds promise about a world where innocence is not lost and love wins, even if it means facing a deadly storm and leaving everything behind to get there.
